text: A single attention head produces one set of weights for each token, so it can follow only one kind of relationship at a time. Language rarely offers just one. In the sentence on the screen, the word sat wants to know who did the sitting, which word came just before it, and where the sitting happened. Multi head attention answers all of these at once, much as a panel of specialists might read the same document, each with their own question, and then pool their notes.

The mechanism is simple. Instead of one head with wide queries and keys, we run several heads side by side, each with its own query, key and value matrices, and each working in a narrower space. If the model width is d and there are h heads, each head gets a width of d divided by h. Every head computes its own scaled, masked attention, completely independently of the others, so each is free to learn its own way of looking.

Each head returns one narrow vector per token. We place these outputs side by side, which restores the full width d, and then multiply by one more learned matrix, the output projection. That final mixing step matters, because it lets the findings of different heads be combined into a single update for each token, rather than sitting in separate compartments.

Splitting the width this way keeps the cost close to that of one wide head, not several times larger. In practice nobody builds the heads one at a time. We compute the queries for all heads with a single matrix product, then reshape the result so that each token's row is cut into h slices, one per head, and swap the axes so that the heads come first. Now one batched matrix multiplication computes every head's score table at once.

Follow the shapes once more. X has T rows and d columns, and so does Q. Reshaping gives T by h by the head width, and swapping the first two axes gives h by T by the head width. The scores become h square tables of T by T, and the outputs are h blocks of T by the head width. Swap the axes back, merge the last two, and we have T by d again, ready for the output projection.

In trained models, different heads do specialise. Some track the previous token, some link words that depend on each other grammatically, and some turn out to be nearly redundant. GPT two small, for example, runs twelve heads in each of its twelve layers. There is one thing every head shares, though: none of them knows where a token sits in the sentence. Attention treats the input as a set, not a sequence, and the next lesson, on positional encoding, fixes that.
